title: Gregory of Valencia agrees: calling and assisting grace
source_text: XXXIII. Atque eodem recidit expositio Gregorii de Valentia. Nam gratiam vocantem, seu excitantem, inquit, appellant Theologi divinas quasdam inspirationes, seu motus quosdam divinitus in mente hominis excitatos, quibus Deus hominem ad se allicit & invitat, & ad actiones pias atque salutares movet, ut fidei, spei, charitatis, & poenitentiae actibus convertatur. Gratiam autem adjuvantem appellant, Dei dona & beneficia, quibus Deus hominem divinae vocationi & excitationi consentientem adjuvat, tum in eo ipso quod consentit & convertitur, tum in aliis actionibus pietatis, per quas contenditur ad beatitudinem. Itaq; ad hanc gratiam adjuvantem in primis pertinet quod Deus peculiari concursu cum homine cooperatur ad conversionem, id est, ad credendum, sperandum, diligendum, poenitendum, &c. Item quod hominem singulari cura & providentia custodit, & protegit a malo, & dirigit atque stimulat ab bonum, & ei variis inspirationibus, ad vincendas tentationes, & ad observanda mandata robur praebet. Tom. 2. disput. 8. quaest. 3. punct. 3.
pass_a_gloss: XXXIII. And to the same comes back the exposition of Gregory of Valencia. For calling grace, or exciting, he says, Theologians call certain divine inspirations, or certain motions divinely excited in the mind of man, by which God allures and invites man to himself, and moves him to pious and salutary actions, that by acts of faith, hope, charity, and repentance he may be converted. But helping grace they call, the gifts and benefits of God, by which God helps man consenting to the divine calling and exciting, both in that very thing that he consents and is converted, and in other actions of piety, through which one strives toward blessedness. And so to this helping grace pertains in the first place that God by a peculiar concurrence cooperates with man to conversion, that is, to believing, hoping, loving, repenting, etc. Likewise that he guards man with singular care and providence, and protects him from evil, and directs and stimulates him to good, and to him by various inspirations, gives strength for conquering temptations, and for observing the commandments. Tom. 2 disput. 8 quaest. 3 punct. 3.
pass_b_english: Thesis XXXIII. Gregory of Valencia's account comes to the same thing. 'Theologians,' he says, 'give the name calling or rousing grace to certain divine inspirations, motions stirred up by God in a man's mind, by which God draws and invites the man to himself and moves him to devout and saving actions, so that he may turn to God by acts of faith, hope, charity and repentance.

They call assisting grace those gifts and benefits by which God helps a man who consents to the divine calling and rousing: both in the very act of consenting and turning, and in the other acts of devotion by which one presses on toward blessedness.

So this assisting grace includes first of all God's special concurrence with man in conversion, that is, in believing, hoping, loving, repenting and so on. It also includes his guarding man with particular care and providence, protecting him from evil, directing and spurring him to good, and giving him strength through various inspirations to overcome temptations and keep the commandments' (tome 2, disputation 8, question 3, point 3).
